content: In the field of chemistry, the standard state of a material is defined as its state at a pressure of exactly 1 bar (100 kilopascals). This definition was updated by IUPAC in 1990. The standard state can be specified at any temperature, but it is most commonly defined at 25 degrees Celsius. However, in some disciplines like physics and engineering, 0 degrees Celsius is often used for Standard Temperature and Pressure (STP). It is important to note that the standard state is an arbitrarily chosen reference point and not a natural zero point. For any given material or substance, the standard state serves as the reference point for thermodynamic properties such as enthalpy, entropy, and Gibbs free energy, as well as for other material standards. The standard enthalpy of formation for an element in its standard state is defined as zero. When referring to a solute in a solution or a chemical reaction, the standard state also includes the condition that the concentrations of all solutes are at unity (or another designated value) for the specified measure of concentration. For molarity, this would mean 1 mol·dm⁻³, and for molality, it would mean 1 mol·kg⁻¹, assuming the solution behaves as if infinitely diluted. If mole fraction is used, the standard state corresponds to the pure liquid or solid (x = 1). It is possible, and theoretically valid, to use different units for each species in a reaction. Therefore, the nature of the standard state must be explicitly specified when reporting or tabulating data. For example, a definition involving 1 mol/L (molarity at unity) of one substance combined with pure mole fraction (x = 1) of another substance represents a condition that cannot physically exist. Nevertheless, such a hypothetical standard state allows for a consistent system of tabulated values, provided it is applied consistently across all calculations. These values will differ from those obtained using a different standard state. The standard state does not imply any specific temperature or pressure, as it is often more practical to describe solutions over a wide range of temperatures and pressures, even if this deviates from IUPAC recommendations. Historically, in the 19th century, the Plimsoll symbol (a superscript o) was adopted to indicate the non-zero nature of the chosen reference state. For typographic reasons, this symbol has often been simplified to a superscript 0 in later texts, which can be misleading.
